title: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography II — the Aksumite gold expedition to Sasu, the silent trade at the thorn hedge, and a Roman merchant's statement of his own sources
language_note:
THIS RECORD CARRIES NO SOURCE-LANGUAGE TEXT AND THE `language_code` SAYS SO. The tier is `published_translation_only` and the only text on the record is McCrindle's English. The Greek of the Christian Topography is not transcribed here, was not captured, and is not claimed — `africa-01-ezana-stone` is the record that shows what happens when a corpus half-claims a text it does not hold, and this one states the position instead.

AND THE FIELD IS OMITTED RATHER THAN FILLED WITH A PLACEHOLDER. `original_text_excerpt` is absent from this record, which raises a sixth loader warning — `empty original_text_excerpt, no original chunk emitted` — and that warning is the honest artefact. date: Written c. 550 CE. Cosmas made his voyages in the reign of Justin I and wrote the Christian Topography under Justinian; McCrindle's edition is dated 1897 and this passage sits at his pages 51–54, in Book II.
reference_translation:
The country known as that of Sasu is itself near the ocean, just as the ocean is near the frankincense country, in which there are many gold mines. The King of the Axômites accordingly, every other year, through the governor of Agau,82 sends thither special agents to bargain for the gold, and these are accompanied by many other traders----upwards, say, of five hundred----bound on the same errand as themselves. They take along with them to the mining district oxen, lumps of salt, and iron, and when they reach its neighbourhood they make a halt at a certain spot and form an encampment, which they fence round with a great hedge of thorns. Within this they live, and having slaughtered the oxen, cut them in |53 pieces, and lay the pieces on the top of the thorns, along with the lumps of salt and the iron. Then come the natives bringing gold in nuggets like peas,83 called tancharas, and lay one or two or more of these upon what pleases them----the pieces of flesh or the salt or the iron, and then they retire to some distance off. Then the owner of the meat approaches, and if he is satisfied he takes the gold away, and upon seeing this its owner comes and takes the flesh or the salt or the iron. If, however, he is not satisfied, he leaves the gold, when the native seeing that he has not taken it, comes and either puts down more gold, or takes up what he had laid down, and goes away. Such is the mode in which business is transacted with the people of that country, because their language is different and interpreters are hardly to be found. The time they stay in that country is five days more or less, according as the natives more or less readily coming forward buy up all their wares. On the journey [140] homeward they all agree to travel well-armed, since some of the tribes through whose country they must pass might threaten to attack them from a desire to rob them of their gold. The space of six months is taken up with this trading expedition, including both the going and the returning. In going they march very slowly, chiefly because of the cattle, but in returning they quicken their pace lest on the way they should be overtaken by winter and its rains. For the sources of the river Nile lie somewhere in these parts, and in winter, on account of the heavy rains, the numerous rivers which they generate obstruct the path of the traveller. The people there have their winter at the time we have our summer. It begins in the month Epiphi of the Egyptians and continues till Thôth,84 and during the |54 three months the rain falls in torrents, and makes a multitude of rivers all of which flow into the Nile.

The facts which I have just recorded fell partly under my own observation and partly were told me by traders who had been to those parts.
reference_translation_note:
J. W. McCrindle's English, 1897, from the transcription served at https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/cosmas_02_book2.htm, read on 2026-09-06. Verified by digest, as records 44, 45 and 46 were: typed on the bridge and sliced independently from the live page in the browser, SHA-256 agreeing at `7f8b6d4d2877ea5095ef66a8…` on 2,777 characters.

EVERY MARK IN IT IS THE EDITION'S OR THE TRANSCRIBER'S AND NONE IS REPAIRED. `82`, `83` and `84` are McCrindle's footnote numbers, left where they fall against `Agau,82` and `peas,83`; `|53` and `|54` are his page boundaries; `[140]` is the transcription's own marker; and the long dashes are rendered as four hyphens, `----`, which is how the 2003 transcription represents them and not how a modern typesetter would.

THE LAST TWO SENTENCES ARE IN THE EXCERPT ON PURPOSE. "The facts which I have just recorded fell partly under my own observation and partly were told me by traders who had been to those parts." **A sixth-century Roman merchant states the boundary of his own knowledge, in the middle of the text, unprompted.** Every record in this corpus is asked to state the boundary of its search; this one holds a source that does the same thing for itself, and it would have been possible to cut the passage one sentence earlier and lose it.

THE BOUNDARY OF THE TRANSLATION SEARCH, AND THIS TIER OWES IT AS MUCH AS ANY OTHER. What was looked at: this transcription of McCrindle 1897, which is the standard English and is out of copyright. What was NOT opened: **Wanda Wolska-Conus's `Topographie chrétienne` (Sources chrétiennes 141, 159, 197, 1968–73)**, the modern critical edition with a French translation, which would give the Greek this record does not carry and a reading later than 1897 — it is in copyright and nothing reachable from this project establishes what it says; and **the manuscripts themselves**, Vaticanus gr. 699 and the Sinai and Florence copies. No claim is made about any of them. THE SEARCH STOPPED AT THE PUBLIC-DOMAIN ENGLISH, which is exactly what a `published_translation_only` record is.

THE SOURCE STATES ITS TERMS AND THE STATEMENT IS THAT THERE ARE NONE TO ENFORCE. Quoted verbatim from the foot of the page:

"This text was transcribed by Roger Pearse, 2003.  All material on this page is in the public domain - copy freely."

Read off https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/cosmas_02_book2.htm on 2026-09-06.

THE POSITION IS `public_domain` AND THIS IS THE FIRST RECORD IN THIS CORPUS TO USE IT. Six of the seven positions in `data/corpus_rights.json` had been exercised and this one had not; it exists because F6 built the column with the full vocabulary rather than with the cases in front of it, and the seventh position — `permission_stated_no_licence` — was added the same day because a case demanded it. **A vocabulary that grows by cases and a vocabulary that waits for them are both visible in this one file now.**

WHY IT IS NOT `open_licence_stated`: no licence is named. A dedication to the public domain is not a licence, and CC0 is not mentioned anywhere reached. WHY IT IS NOT `states_no_terms`: the source states terms — it states that the material is in the public domain and invites copying, which is a position and not a silence.

AND THE UNDERLYING WORK IS OUT OF COPYRIGHT ON ITS OWN: McCrindle died in 1913 and the translation was published in 1897. Ruling 74's four conditions are not needed here and are not invoked; this record is the case ruling 74 was written to be able to distinguish itself FROM.

WHAT THE START DOCUMENT EXPECTED AND WHY THIS IS NOT IT. `F6_CURATION_START.md` §4 said this slot would come from `noorlib.ir`, which "is open (browser pass 2) and states no licence, so ruling 74's third condition applies in the form it prescribes". **It did not come from there.** `noorlib.ir` is a commercial library serving Arabic and Persian works, and what this tier needs is a published ENGLISH translation, which that site does not supply. The expectation was written before the tier's requirement was checked against the site's content, and it is recorded here rather than quietly dropped.
findspot: Not applicable — a transmitted literary text. The Christian Topography survives in Vaticanus gr. 699 and later copies; this record holds an English translation of Book II and no manuscript witness.
notes:
F6, the Sub-Saharan Africa `published_translation_only` slot — the last of F6's seven and, as the allocation intended, the cheapest.

WHAT IT ADDS THAT AFRICA DID NOT HAVE. The corpus's Africa records are a Greek inscription of an Aksumite king, a Greek inscription of a Nubian king, a Greek periplus, a British Museum coin, a placeholder, and — as of today — a Ge'ez royal inscription. **None of them is about trade going INLAND.** This passage is: it follows an Aksumite state expedition, sent every other year through the governor of Agau, five hundred traders strong, carrying oxen, salt and iron six months into the interior to exchange them for gold at a hedge of thorns, with neither side speaking the other's language. `africa-03-periplus-adulis` shows the Roman world's goods arriving at the coast; this shows what the kingdom behind that coast was doing with them.

AND THE ROMAN CONNECTION IS THE AUTHOR, NOT THE SUBJECT. Cosmas is an Alexandrian merchant of the empire, writing in Greek in Justinian's reign, who had been to Adulis himself — `africa-05-adulis-throne` exists because he copied the Monumentum Adulitanum there. **This record is the same man's own narrative**, which the corpus previously held only at one remove, as the vehicle for somebody else's inscription.

THIS IS A RECORD WHERE AFRICA IS SPOKEN ABOUT, AND THAT IS THE TIER WORKING AS DESIGNED. It adds nothing to the `SPEAKING` subtotal FINDING 68 built and it is not meant to: `published_translation_only` does not count toward the per-region source-language floor, which Africa closed this morning with `africa-06-ezana-rie189`. The two records were curated the same day, on purpose, and they are the two halves of the question the provenance line asks.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE. F6's one declaration is ruling 77's and is spent on `arabia-07-cih541`. The material is thin here in any case: McCrindle's `tancharas` is transliterated rather than translated, and the identification of Sasu is a live question this record does not enter.

THE TIER IS NOW 2 OF 4 AT 60 RECORDS. It stood at 1 — `africa-01-ezana-stone`, which is a placeholder and a newspaper citation — and this is the second, which is a public-domain scholarly translation of a named book with a named translator and a page range. **The tier's two members are a fair picture of how far this project's standards moved between its seed corpus and Block F**, and that comparison is worth more than the count.

subject_places.name: Sasu — the gold country the expedition goes to
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND THE SOURCE PLACES IT ONLY BY RELATION. The text says Sasu "is itself near the ocean, just as the ocean is near the frankincense country" and calls it, earlier in the same book, "the remotest part of Ethiopia". Its modern identification is a scholarly question — the Sudanese-Ethiopian borderlands and the Blue Nile region are both argued — and this record has opened no commentary on it. PHASE2's W1 rule forbids authoring a coordinate, and a focus with no id is what an unlocated centre of gravity looks like.

subject_places.name: The kingdom of the Axômites — where the expedition sets out from
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND SPECIFICALLY PLEIADES 39303 `A(u)xoume` IS NOT IMPORTED, THOUGH THIS CORPUS HOLDS IT AND USED IT TWICE TODAY. The text names `the King of the Axômites` — a PEOPLE and their king, not the city — and the expedition is dispatched `through the governor of Agau`, from no named place. `africa-06-ezana-rie189` takes the Aksum id because its source states the findspot of a stone; this record has no stone and no stated city, and the same corpus rule that refused an id for `kēsar`, for `Hrōmāy` and for `mlk Rmn` refuses one here. THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO AFRICA RECORDS CURATED TODAY IS INSTRUCTIVE AND IS WHY THIS NOTE IS LONG.

subject_places.name: Barbaria, the frankincense country along the ocean
subject_places.note: NO ID. Named in the same sentence as Sasu and used to locate it. `arabia-01-periplus` carries a `frankincense country` on the OTHER side of the Red Sea and the two must not be collapsed: this one is the projecting part of the Horn, and the corpus now holds both under names their own sources give them.

subject_places.name: The Nile, whose sources the text places in these parts
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND THE CLAIM IS THE SOURCE'S. "For the sources of the river Nile lie somewhere in these parts" — a sixth-century Alexandrian locating the Nile's sources in the gold country of the interior. Recorded as `mentioned` because nothing moves along it in this passage; the rains that raise it are what turn the traders back.
